Stack.description: Ah, the LAMP stack — the granddaddy of them all. Linux keeps the lights on (literally, it IS the light), Apache serves your pages like a tireless waiter who never takes a break, MySQL remembers everything you've ever told it in neat little rows and columns, and PHP... well, PHP ties it all together with the enthusiasm of a developer who discovered string concatenation and never looked back. Together, they power roughly half the internet, including every WordPress blog your aunt has ever started and abandoned.

externalAttribution.note: Kunze deliberately coined the acronym as a marketing device for free/open-source software.

Stack.description: The MEAN stack is what happens when JavaScript developers look at the server and say 'we can take that too.' MongoDB stores your data as JSON (because everything is JSON now), Express handles routing with the quiet competence of a librarian, Angular builds your frontend with more decorators than a Christmas tree, and Node.js ties it all together by running JavaScript on the server — something that was once considered a war crime. It's JavaScript all the way down, which is either brilliant or terrifying depending on your relationship with callback functions.

externalAttribution.note: Karpov was a Node.js engineer at MongoDB. He coined it saying: 'My team uses a set of tools that we affectionately call the MEAN stack.'
externalAttribution.source: Blog post: 'The MEAN Stack' on thecodebarbarian.com

questionnaire.notableFeature: React's component model for building UIs

Stack.description: MERN is MEAN's cooler younger sibling who showed up to the party wearing React instead of Angular and immediately became more popular. MongoDB still stores your documents, Express still routes your requests, and Node.js still runs your server — but React brings the component-based UI magic that makes frontend developers feel like they're building with Lego instead of wrestling with spaghetti. It dominates bootcamp curricula worldwide, which means roughly 40% of all junior developer portfolios are built on it.

externalAttribution.note: Natural evolution from MEAN as React surpassed Angular in popularity. No single coiner identified.

questionnaire.industries: Web applications requiring relational data integrity
questionnaire.notableFeature: PostgreSQL's relational power with React's UI model

Stack.description: PERN is for developers who looked at MERN and said 'I love everything about this except the part where my data has no schema.' PostgreSQL brings actual relational integrity — foreign keys, constraints, the works — while Express and Node.js handle the server side and React makes the frontend sparkle. It's the responsible adult version of the JavaScript full-stack, chosen by teams who've been burned by MongoDB's 'eh, just throw it in a document' approach one too many times.

questionnaire.notableFeature: Full-text search across all your logs

Stack.description: The ELK stack is what happens when you have so many logs that you need a search engine just to find out what went wrong at 3 AM. Elasticsearch indexes everything faster than you can say 'why is the server on fire,' Logstash ingests data from approximately nine thousand different sources and transforms it into something useful, and Kibana turns all that chaos into beautiful dashboards that make your ops team look like they know what they're doing. Used by Netflix, eBay, and every SRE who's ever been paged at dinner.

externalAttribution.note: Officially rebranded to 'Elastic Stack' in 2016 to accommodate Beats, but everyone still calls it ELK.
externalAttribution.source: Community-coined after the three creators joined Elastic

questionnaire.industries: Rapid web application development, Laravel ecosystem

Stack.description: The TALL stack is the Laravel community's answer to JavaScript fatigue. Tailwind CSS makes your HTML look like someone spilled a Scrabble board on it but somehow it comes out beautiful, Alpine.js adds just enough interactivity without requiring a build step, Laravel provides the most elegant PHP framework known to humanity, and Livewire lets you build reactive UIs entirely in PHP — because who needs a JavaScript framework when you have Caleb Porzio's sheer force of will? It's full-stack development for people who actually like PHP.

externalAttribution.note: Porzio created both Alpine.js and Livewire, making him the most likely originator.

Stack.description: The BETH stack is the hipster cousin who showed up to Thanksgiving dinner and won't stop talking about how we've been doing web development wrong for fifteen years. Bun runs your JavaScript faster than Node ever could (and lets you know about it), Elysia serves your routes with TypeScript-first elegance, Turso keeps your SQLite database at the edge because latency is the enemy, and HTMX lets you build interactive UIs by... writing HTML attributes. That's it. No virtual DOM, no hydration, no build step — just good old hypermedia the way Tim Berners-Lee intended.

questionnaire.notableFeature: Real-time server-rendered UIs on the BEAM VM

Stack.description: The PETAL stack is what you get when Erlang's battle-tested concurrency model puts on a beautiful dress and goes to a web development party. Phoenix handles your web layer with Rails-like productivity, Elixir makes functional programming feel friendly, Tailwind CSS keeps things pretty, Alpine.js adds client-side sprinkles, and LiveView — the real star — lets you build real-time interactive UIs with server-rendered HTML pushed over WebSockets. No JavaScript framework needed. Your app can handle two million simultaneous connections on a single server, which is probably overkill for your todo app but very impressive at parties.

questionnaire.industries: Graph-heavy applications, knowledge management, social networks
questionnaire.notableFeature: Graph database with GraphQL API — graphs all the way down

Stack.description: The GRAND stack is for developers who realized their data is more about relationships than rows. GraphQL lets your frontend ask for exactly what it needs (no more, no less), React renders it beautifully, Apollo manages the data layer with caching that actually works, and Neo4j stores everything as nodes and edges because your data is a graph whether you admit it or not. It's particularly popular for recommendation engines, fraud detection, and that social network you're definitely going to build someday.

externalAttribution.note: Lyon was Staff Developer Advocate at Neo4j.

questionnaire.industries: Enterprise web applications in the .NET/F# ecosystem
questionnaire.notableFeature: End-to-end F# — functional programming from server to browser

Stack.description: The SAFE stack is functional programming's answer to full-stack web development, and it's entirely in F#. Saturn provides the server framework with an elegant computation expression API, Azure hosts it all in Microsoft's cloud, Fable compiles your F# to JavaScript (because why would you write JavaScript when you could write F# instead?), and Elmish brings the Elm architecture to your frontend. It's type-safe from database to DOM, which means if it compiles, it probably works. The F# community is small but fierce, and SAFE is their crown jewel.

questionnaire.industries: Modern Python web applications, APIs, data science frontends
questionnaire.notableFeature: FastAPI's automatic OpenAPI docs and async Python

Stack.description: The FARM stack is what happens when Python developers finally get a web framework that's as fast as they always claimed Python could be. FastAPI serves your API with automatic documentation, type validation, and async support that makes Flask look like it's running on a hamster wheel. React handles the frontend because what else would you use, and MongoDB stores your data as documents because your Python dicts were basically JSON anyway. It's the modern Python web stack for people who want type hints, speed, and zero boilerplate.

questionnaire.notableFeature: Firebase's real-time database and zero-config auth

Stack.description: The FERN stack is MERN's cloud-native cousin who traded self-hosted MongoDB for Firebase and never looked back. Firebase handles auth, real-time database, hosting, and approximately seventeen other things you'd otherwise have to set up yourself. Express and Node.js do the server-side heavy lifting, and React builds the UI. It's the stack of choice for hackathons, MVPs, and that side project you're going to ship this weekend (you won't, but Firebase makes it feel possible).

The AEFS stack is a modern full-stack architecture that separates concerns across the frontend state layer, backend API logic, and deployment infrastructure. **Elmish** handles all client-side state management and UI rendering, providing a functional, event-driven architecture that keeps the frontend predictable and testable. This feeds into **FastAPI**, which serves as the core business logic layer—a high-performance Python framework that processes requests, orchestrates domain logic, and exposes a clean REST or GraphQL interface. **Saturn** sits between these layers as a specialized routing and middleware orchestrator, managing request lifecycle, authentication flows, and cross-cutting concerns like logging and validation before they hit FastAPI's handlers. Finally, **Apache** provides the HTTP server foundation and reverse proxy layer, handling SSL termination, load balancing, and static asset serving at the edge. This layering allows teams to scale each component independently: the frontend can be rebuilt without touching the backend, FastAPI can be load-balanced horizontally, and Apache can be tuned for throughput without affecting business logic.

The stack's strength lies in its clean separation of responsibilities and language diversity. Elmish brings functional reactive patterns to the client, while FastAPI leverages Python's ecosystem for rapid backend development. Saturn acts as the glue layer, allowing you to decouple frontend state changes from backend implementation details—requests flow through Saturn's middleware chain for enrichment before reaching FastAPI handlers. Apache ensures that whatever load your application receives hits a battle-tested, tunable HTTP server. This isn't a "batteries included" monolith; it's a deliberate choice to use the right tool at each layer, with clear interfaces between them.

# The PPBA Stack

The PPBA stack is a full-stack JavaScript and backend architecture designed for applications that need both lightweight edge computing and a robust persistent data layer. **Bun** serves as our primary JavaScript runtime and build tool, handling all frontend tooling, package management, and server-side JavaScript execution with superior performance compared to Node.js. **Angular** is our frontend framework, providing a comprehensive, opinionated structure for complex single-page applications with built-in dependency injection, RxJS reactivity, and strong TypeScript support. This frontend layer communicates with our backend services via REST or gRPC APIs, allowing us to maintain a clear separation of concerns.

On the backend, **PHP** handles our business logic and API endpoints, leveraging its mature ecosystem of frameworks and libraries for rapid feature development. PHP runs as a FastCGI service behind a reverse proxy, processing requests that come from the Angular frontend or other clients. **PostgreSQL** is our source of truth—a powerful relational database that handles all persistent data storage, complex queries, and ACID compliance requirements that our application demands. The PHP backend connects directly to PostgreSQL, managing migrations, transactions, and data integrity while exposing cleaned, filtered data through well-defined API contracts.

This hybrid approach lets teams maximize developer productivity: frontend engineers work in a modern, unified TypeScript environment with Bun and Angular, while backend engineers leverage PHP's rapid iteration cycles and PostgreSQL's reliability. API contracts are defined upfront, enabling parallel development streams. Bun's performance benefits the build pipeline and any Node-based tooling, while PHP's stability and library depth remain proven for handling complex server-side operations.

# The ARAL Stack

The ARAL stack combines our frontend frameworks with centralized logging to deliver a resilient, observable web application. We use Angular as our primary application framework for complex, stateful views that require sophisticated dependency injection and TypeScript-first development. React handles our component library and isolated UI features that benefit from a virtual DOM approach, allowing us to maintain both architectures without conflict by keeping them in separate application domains. Alpine.js provides lightweight interactivity for server-rendered pages and progressive enhancement where we don't need the overhead of a full framework, keeping our initial page loads fast and our bundle sizes reasonable.

On the infrastructure side, Logstash aggregates logs from all three frontend frameworks, our Node backend services, and application events into a centralized pipeline. Every user interaction, error, and state change flows through Logstash, which parses, enriches, and forwards the data to our ELK stack for real-time monitoring and historical analysis. This unified logging layer gives us complete visibility into how Angular, React, and Alpine.js are performing across the application, letting us quickly identify bottlenecks and debug issues in production. The separation of frameworks is intentional—each handles the part of the application where it excels, while Logstash ensures we never lose observability across the entire system.

# The DEULEY Stack

The DEULEY stack is a modern full-stack architecture designed for applications that require sophisticated backend logic, responsive frontend experiences, and blockchain integration. Django serves as our core web framework, handling API endpoints, business logic, and server-side rendering with the reliability and speed required when you're shipping on deadline. We pair this with Ember.js on the frontend, which provides the structure and conventions we need to build ambitious, stateful web applications without constant context-switching between architectural paradigms.

Our Python ecosystem is managed through uv, a high-performance package manager that keeps our Django dependencies locked and reproducible while dramatically reducing installation times across our development and CI/CD pipelines. On the application side, LangChain enables us to build agentic features—RAG pipelines, autonomous workflows, and AI-powered decision-making—directly within our Django views and background tasks, giving us sophisticated AI capabilities without maintaining a separate services layer.

For our blockchain infrastructure, we run Ethereum as our settlement layer and smart contract platform, allowing us to offer users transparent, cryptographically-verified transactions and on-chain state management where it matters. JavaScript dependencies and build tooling are coordinated through Yarn, which ensures deterministic installs and seamless integration with our Ember.js frontend build pipeline. Together, these components create a coherent system: a traditional web application backed by intelligent agents and secured by distributed ledger verification.

# The TACO Stack

The TACO stack is a full-featured architecture designed for applications that require real-time communications alongside sophisticated graph-based data retrieval. At its core, Tomcat serves as the application server, hosting our REST APIs and handling HTTP request routing. It's lightweight, battle-tested, and gives us fine-grained control over deployment and resource management. Tomcat connects to both our communication layer and our persistent data stores, making it the natural orchestration point for the entire system.

Asterisk handles all telephony and real-time communication features, whether that's VoIP call routing, IVR systems, or SIP protocol management. Our Tomcat application servers communicate with Asterisk via AMI (Asterisk Manager Interface) or REST endpoints when we need to initiate calls, transfer sessions, or log call metadata. This separation of concerns keeps our business logic clean while Asterisk focuses on what it does best: managing complex communication workflows at scale.

Our data layer uses Oracle DB for transactional data and operational records, while Cypher running against a property graph database handles relationship-heavy queries—think social networks, recommendation engines, or call routing decision trees. When the application needs to determine the optimal call path based on customer history, network relationships, or service dependencies, it queries the graph via Cypher. For consistent, ACID-compliant transactional data like billing records and user accounts, we write to Oracle. This dual-database approach lets us optimize for the query patterns each workload demands without compromise.

# The LLLL Stack

The LLLL stack pairs Laravel with Livewire for rapid full-stack web development, while leveraging LangChain and Lisp for specialized computational workloads. Laravel serves as our primary application framework, handling HTTP routing, database orchestration, and business logic in a familiar, expressive environment. Livewire sits on top of Laravel to eliminate context-switching between frontend and backend—it gives us reactive, dynamic UIs without writing JavaScript, keeping the entire application within Laravel's PHP ecosystem.

For operations requiring complex reasoning or agent-based workflows, we delegate to LangChain, our agent engineering platform. LangChain handles the coordination of language models, memory management, and tool integration—essentially running autonomous decision-making loops that the Laravel application can invoke via API calls. When LangChain needs to perform heavy symbolic computation or maintain high-performance constraint solving, it spawns isolated Lisp processes using Steel Bank Common Lisp. Lisp's macro system and native support for symbolic manipulation make it ideal for the kinds of logical reasoning tasks that would otherwise bottleneck LangChain's Python runtime.

The architecture keeps concerns cleanly separated: Laravel and Livewire own the user-facing application and request handling, LangChain manages agentic AI workflows, and Lisp provides a performant execution layer for computationally intensive symbolic work. Communication flows through well-defined API boundaries, allowing each component to scale independently while remaining simple to reason about.

# The UNI Stack

The UNI stack is a modern, graph-native architecture built on Ubuntu, Neo4j, and Istio. Ubuntu serves as our foundational operating system across all nodes in the cluster, providing a stable, hardened Linux environment where our containerized services run. Neo4j handles our primary data layer, storing and querying complex, highly-connected datasets as a native graph database. This choice lets us model relationships between entities—users, transactions, permissions, recommendations—as first-class citizens rather than expensive joins, which is critical for the real-time queries our platform demands. Istio sits at the service mesh layer, managing all inter-service communication, encryption, and observability across the cluster.

The three components work together deliberately. As services deployed on Ubuntu containers need to communicate with each other and with Neo4j, Istio intercepts and governs that traffic without requiring changes to application code. It handles service-to-service authentication, enforces network policies, and gives us distributed tracing across all calls to the graph database. Neo4j's Cypher queries often fan out across multiple microservices—pulling related data from different domains—so Istio's traffic management, retry logic, and circuit breaking become essential for reliability. Ubuntu underpins everything, ensuring consistent kernel behavior, security patches, and container runtime stability across development, staging, and production environments.

This stack is particularly effective for applications where relationship queries and service interdependency are both high. We chose it because we needed a database that thinks in graphs, an operating system we could standardize on, and a service mesh that would give us observability and control without rewriting our services. It's not a one-size-fits-all choice, but for this workload, the three components complement each other naturally.

# The KIL Stack

The KIL stack is our event-driven data analytics platform, built around three core components that handle ingestion, computation, and infrastructure. **Kafka** serves as the backbone of the system, ingesting streams of data from distributed sources and maintaining a persistent, replicated log that allows us to process events at scale. It decouples our data producers from consumers, giving us flexibility to add new analytics workloads without disrupting the pipeline. We run Kafka clusters across multiple nodes to handle throughput in the gigabytes-per-second range.

**IPython** is our interactive computation and analysis layer, where data engineers and scientists develop transformations, validate hypotheses, and prototype new features against the Kafka streams. We've containerized IPython instances that connect directly to our Kafka brokers, allowing teams to write Python code that consumes and transforms event data in real time. This gives us a fast feedback loop during development while keeping experimental work isolated from production consumers.

The entire stack runs on **Linux** infrastructure—our Kafka brokers, IPython containers, and supporting services all operate on hardened Linux distributions optimized for networking and I/O performance. Linux gives us the process isolation, scheduling control, and system observability we need to run both the streaming platform and interactive workloads reliably. By controlling the kernel layer directly, we can tune network buffers and tune CPU affinity for Kafka brokers to maximize throughput, while maintaining the flexibility IPython needs for development and debugging.
